title: Family — and the verb "to have"
goal: Name family members, say who you have, ask someone's age — and use both ways Persian has of saying who owns what.
bekal: use داشتن ("to have") for family, things, and age
shorten کتابِ من to کتابم with a possessive ending
describe family relations that Persian has no single word for

dialogs.title: گفتگو — عکسِ خانواده
dialogs.intro: Maryam opens her phone and shows Budi an old photo.

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.id: This is a photo of my family.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.id: What a big family! How many of you are there?

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.text: ما شش نفریم: پدر، مادر، دو برادر، یک خواهر و من.
lines.baca: mâ shesh nafarim: pedar, mâdar, do barâdar, yek khâhar va man.
lines.id: There are six of us: my father, my mother, two brothers, one sister, and me.
lines.literal: we six person-we: father, mother, two brother, one sister and I.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: برادرِ بزرگ‌ترِ شما چند سال دارد؟
lines.baca: barâdar-e bozorgtar-e shomâ chand sâl dârad?
lines.id: How old is your older brother?
lines.literal: brother-of bigger-of you how-many year has-he?

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.text: سی و دو سال. اسمش علی است و مهندس است.
lines.baca: si o do sâl. esmash Ali ast va mohandes ast.
lines.id: Thirty-two. His name is Ali and he's an engineer.
lines.literal: thirty and two year. name-his Ali is and engineer is.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: و آن خانمِ کنارِ پدرتان کیست؟
lines.baca: va ân khânom-e kenâr-e pedaretân kist?
lines.id: And who is the lady next to your father?
lines.literal: and that lady-of side-of father-your who-is?

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.text: آن مادربزرگم است. نودساله است و خیلی سرحال.
lines.baca: ân mâdarbozorgam ast. navad-sâle ast va kheyli sarhâl.
lines.id: That's my grandmother. She's ninety and still very fit.
lines.literal: that mother-big-my is. ninety-year-old is and very fit.

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.text: بله، یک دختر دارم. اسمش نرگس است.
lines.baca: bale, yek dokhtar dâram. esmash Narges ast.
lines.id: Yes, I have a daughter. Her name is Narges.
lines.literal: yes, one daughter have-I. name-her Narges is.

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.text: پنج سالش است. شما خواهر و برادر دارید؟
lines.baca: panj sâlash ast. shomâ khâhar o barâdar dârid?
lines.id: She's five. Do you have brothers or sisters?
lines.literal: five year-her is. you sister and brother have-you?

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: یک خواهرِ کوچک‌تر دارم. برادر ندارم.
lines.baca: yek khâhar-e kuchaktar dâram. barâdar nadâram.
lines.id: I have a younger sister. I don't have a brother.
lines.literal: one sister-of smaller have-I. brother not-have-I.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: در جاکارتا. دلم برایشان تنگ است.
lines.baca: dar Jâkârtâ. delam barâyeshân tang ast.
lines.literal: in Jakarta. heart-my for-them narrow is.

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.text: می‌فهمم. خانواده همیشه در دل است.
lines.baca: mifahmam. khânevâde hamishe dar del ast.
lines.id: I understand. Family is always in your heart.
lines.literal: understand-I. family always in heart is.

notes: ⚠️ **Persian has no single word for "older brother" or "younger sister".** Just like English, there is only برادر (brother) and خواهر (sister), with no age built in. If you need the difference, add it yourself: برادرِ بزرگ‌تر ("older brother", literally "bigger brother") and خواهرِ کوچک‌تر ("younger sister", literally "smaller sister"). Many languages of Asia — Indonesian, Korean, Chinese — make this distinction compulsory; Persian, like English, mentions age only when it matters.

⚠️ **Age is expressed with "have", not "be".** چند سال دارید؟ is literally "how many years do you have?" — the same way French and Spanish do it. An equally common second way uses a possessive ending: چند سالتان است؟ ("how-many year-your is?"). Both are correct and you'll hear both often. The answer: سی سال دارم or سی سالم است.

⚠️ **The verb داشتن never takes the prefix می.** Its present tense is دارم، داری، دارد، داریم، دارید، دارند — there is no می‌دارم. Together with بودن, it is the only important verb that behaves this way, and می‌دارم is one of the mistakes most often heard from beginners. The negative: ندارم، نداری، ندارد and so on.

**Shortening اسمِ او gives اسمش.** The ending ـش attaches straight to the noun and replaces the whole ezafe chain. کتابم = کتابِ من, خانه‌ات = خانهٔ تو, مادرش = مادرِ او. Both forms mean the same; the ending is shorter and more common in conversation.

**Grandma is "big mother": مادربزرگ, and grandpa is پدربزرگ, "big father".** Persian builds family words from pieces you already know, much like English *grandmother* or *stepfather*. The same pattern: برادرزاده ("brother-born" = nephew/niece), خواهرزاده, همسر ("co-head" = spouse).

**In the family it's always تو.** To parents, siblings, children, and close friends, Iranians use تو. Using شما with your own brother sounds like you are having a fight. Outside that circle — neighbors, shopkeepers, bosses, new people — always شما.

grammars.title: داشتن — to have
body: The second most important verb in Persian after بودن. It expresses possession, age, need, and dozens of other combinations — and it does **not** take the prefix می in the present.
after: Notice that the endings are exactly the same as the "be" endings in unit 1: ـم، ـی، ـد، ـیم، ـید، ـند. Learn these six once and you have them for **every** Persian verb — there is no second set to memorize.
The negative is formed with the prefix **نـ**: دارم → ندارم. The same rule applies to every verb, and you'll meet it again in unit 9.
Tehran speech: دارم (*dâram*), داری (*dâri*), **داره** (*dâre*), داریم (*dârim*), **دارین** (*dârin*), **دارن** (*dâran*). Notice ـد → ـه and ـید → ـین; both shifts apply to every verb.

grammars.title: Possessive endings — the second way to say "my"
body: Besides ezafe (کتابِ من), Persian has a shortcut: six endings attached directly to the noun. The meaning is exactly the same, but the form is shorter and far more common in conversation.
after: **After a vowel, a linker is inserted:** خانه → خانه‌ام (*khâne-am*, "my house"), خانه‌ات، خانه‌اش. If this form makes you hesitate, just use the long form — خانهٔ من is always right.
Tehran speech shortens the last three: کتابمون (*ketâbemun*), کتابتون (*ketâbetun*), کتابشون (*ketâbeshun*).

⚠️ These possessive endings **look almost identical** to the "be" endings from unit 1 — کتابم could mean "my book" or "I am a book". What tells them apart is the kind of word: on a noun it's possession; on an adjective or a job it's "am". معلمم = "I'm a teacher", کتابم = "my book". In practice the sentence is never really ambiguous.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice the four words for "uncle" and "aunt": Persian **separates** the father's side from the mother's side (عمو and دایی, عمه and خاله), while English does not. It works the other way with brothers and sisters: in one place Persian is more detailed than English, in another it is just as loose. No language is more complete than another — each simply cuts up the world in different places.

blocks.title: همسر — one word for husband and wife
items: The word همسر (*hamsar*) is literally "co-head", from هم ("same, co-") + سر ("head"). It means husband **or** wife and is used in formal and polite settings — just like English "spouse" or "partner".

The prefix هم is productive: هم‌کلاس ("classmate"), هم‌خانه ("housemate"), هم‌کار ("co-worker"), هم‌وطن ("compatriot"). It works much like English *co-* or *-mate*, and you can guess the meaning every time.

blocks.title: Four sentences for talking about your family
items: "There are ... of us." — ما ... نفریم. (*mâ ... nafarim.*)
"I have one sister and two brothers." — یک خواهر و دو برادر دارم. (*yek khâhar va do barâdar dâram.*)
"I don't have children. / I have a daughter." — من بچه ندارم. / یک دختر دارم. (*man bache nadâram. / yek dokhtar dâram.*)
"My parents live in Indonesia." — پدر و مادرم در اندونزی زندگی می‌کنند. (*pedar o mâdaram dar Andonezi zendegi mikonand.*) This last verb is taken apart in unit 9; for now, learn it whole.

exercises.prompt: Change the long form into the short form with a possessive ending.
Fill in the right form of داشتن.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: من یک خواهرِ کوچک‌تر دارم. — من برادر ندارم. — شما بچه دارید؟ — چند سال دارید؟ — من بیست و پنج سال دارم.
من یک خواهر دارم. — من برادر ندارم. — شما بچه دارید؟ — پنج سالش است. — او سی سال دارد.
